n: In this lecture we will examine toxic compounds containing silver, copper, manganese and chromium, and the methods for their analysis. Key words: silver, copper, manganese, chromium. The aim of the lecture is for you to become familiar with the scheme for examining a mineralisate for compounds of silver, copper, manganese and chromium.

First, the uses of silver compounds. In medicine, silver nitrate is used as a cauterising agent, that is, in the form of the lunar caustic stick. Collargol and protargol are used as astringent or antiseptic agents. Silver preparations are also found in photography, in mirror making and in hair dyeing. Because these compounds easily reach the hands of the public, there is a risk of poisoning. Remember: silver oxide, chloride, bromide and iodide are insoluble in water and are not considered toxic.

Now, silver poisoning. In poisoning the skin takes on a grey-green tint. Silver is eliminated from the body mainly through the large intestine. If dust of silver salts enters through the respiratory tract, the capillaries are damaged. Silver accumulates in the tissues for a long time; this condition is called argyria. As a result the skin is stained a bluish-grey colour.

The preliminary reaction in detecting silver is carried out with dithizone. To 5 ml of mineralisate, 5 ml of chloroform and 2-3 drops of a 0.02% chloroform solution of dithizone are added and the mixture is shaken. If silver is present, the layer turns yellow-golden. Mercury gives the same colour, that is, it interferes. To distinguish them, the mixture is shaken with 0.5 N HCl. Silver dithizonate decomposes and the green colour of dithizone appears. Mercury dithizonate does not decompose and the colour persists.

The next step is precipitating silver with NaCl. 0.5 g of NaCl is added to 100 ml of mineralisate. If no precipitate forms, it is kept at 80°C for 2 hours, then left for 1 day. The precipitate is filtered off, and the filtrate is used for the analysis of other elements. The precipitate on the filter is washed with 0.5 N HCl, with water and finally with 8 N NH4OH. As a result, AgCl is converted into the ammonia complex.

t: Conversion of AgCl into the ammonia complex
n: This slide shows the conversion of AgCl into the ammonia complex. The precipitate on the filter is washed with 0.5 N HCl, with water and finally with 8 N NH4OH. Under the action of ammonia, AgCl dissolves and the silver ammonia complex is formed. The reaction is as follows: AgCl and 2 NH4OH give [Ag(NH3)2]Cl and 2 H2O. With the resulting solution, the recrystallisation, HNO3, KI and picrate reactions are performed.

t: Confirmatory reactions of silver ammonia complex
n: There are three confirmatory reactions of the silver ammonia complex. The first is recrystallisation: if 1-2 drops of the solution are evaporated at room temperature, octahedral and tetrahedral crystals are seen under the microscope. The second is with nitric acid: a white precipitate of AgCl forms. The third is with a saturated solution of potassium iodide: a yellow precipitate of AgI forms.

The picrate reaction of silver. After the silver ammonia complex is evaporated on a microscope slide, saturated solutions of thiourea and potassium picrate are added to the residue. As a result, yellow prismatic crystal aggregates form. With rubidium and gold salts, red prismatic crystals of AgCl·AuCl3·6RbCl form. The amount of silver is determined by the volumetric method: titration with ammonium thiocyanate, using a ferric salt as the indicator.

Now, the uses of copper compounds. They are used in paint manufacture, in porcelain production and in agriculture for pest control. CuO, CuSO3, Cu(OH)2, that is, malachite, CuSO4 and CuCl2 are used in fabric printing and in electroplating. In medicine, copper sulphate, copper citrate and organic compounds such as cuprex are used.

On copper-containing pesticides. TCPC, that is, copper trichlorophenolate, is used for dressing cotton seed. Schweinfurt green and Paris green are used to control agricultural pests and malaria-carrying mosquitoes. Schweinfurt green is written Cu(CH3COO)2·3Cu(AsO2)2, and Paris green is written Cu2As2O3. Remember: along with copper, they also contain arsenic.

Copper poisoning proceeds as follows. The absorption of copper compounds from the stomach into the blood is slow, and they are expelled with the vomit. As a result of absorption, diarrhoea occurs. Haemolysis takes place in the blood vessels. The copper ion is eliminated from the body mainly through the intestine and the kidneys.

Toxic doses of copper sulphate. The smallest amount of copper sulphate capable of a strong effect is about 0.6 g. 1-2 grams poison and may even cause death. According to some authors, the lethal dose of CuSO4 is 10 g. In poisoning, severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and bloody diarrhoea are observed. Body temperature reaches 38-40°, and nosebleed occurs.

t: Isolating copper as the DDTC complex
n: The main method of isolating copper is extraction as the DDTC complex. From the mineralisate, copper is extracted with chloroform as copper diethyldithiocarbamate. Then HgCl2 is added and mercury DDTC is formed. The copper ion passes into the aqueous layer. That is, the copper in the chloroform is replaced by mercury.

Decomposing Cu-DDTC with mercury. From the mineralisate, copper is extracted with chloroform as diethyldithiocarbamate, that is, as the DDTC complex. The chloroform layer is decomposed with a solution of HgCl2: mercury DDTC is formed, and the copper ion passes into the aqueous layer. The reaction involves Cu(DDTC)2 in chloroform and 1% HgCl2. The products are Hg(DDTC)2 in chloroform and CuCl2 in the aqueous layer. HgCl2 is added dropwise until the colour disappears. The aqueous layer is separated and tested for copper.

The procedure for isolating copper has five steps. Step one, the indicator: 2-3 drops of 2,4-dinitrophenol are added to the mineralisate, and 25% ammonia is added dropwise until a yellow colour appears, that is, pH = 3. Step two, extraction: in a separating funnel, shake with 5 ml of a chloroform solution of lead DDTC; if the layer is yellow-brown, it is separated. Step three, washing: the chloroform layer is washed with 6 N HCl, then with water. Step four, decomposition: 1% HgCl2 is added dropwise until the colour disappears. Step five: shake with 1-2 ml of water, and test the aqueous layer for copper.

Confirmatory reactions of copper. With ammonium tetrathiocyanatomercurate, a yellow-green precipitate forms. If Zn2+ is added, a red-pink, that is, lilac, precipitate appears. With yellow prussiate of potash K4[Fe(CN)6], red-brown Cu2[Fe(CN)6] forms. If Cd2+ is added, a lilac colour appears. Remember: iron, cobalt and nickel also form a precipitate of such a colour with tetrathiocyanatomercurate.

t: Detecting copper with pyridine thiocyanate; quantification
n: Detecting copper with the pyridine thiocyanate reagent. A precipitate forms with the reagent. If chloroform is added, the precipitate dissolves and the layer turns emerald green. The amount of copper is determined as diethyldithiocarbamate by the photoelectrocolorimetric method, that is, the PEC method. Another way is the volumetric method: titration with Trilon B, the indicator is murexide, and the colour changes from yellow to red.

Uses of manganese compounds. They are used in making electrodes, in glass production, in preparing enamels and glazes, and in other branches of the chemical industry. KMnO4 is used in medicine as a disinfectant. Poisoning is quite common in industry and in everyday life.

The action and signs of manganese poisoning. Manganese compounds not only affect internal organs such as the kidneys and lungs, but also disable the central nervous system. Signs: burning in the mouth, nausea, vomiting, pain in the stomach and abdomen. The throat is stained brown, and signs of parkinsonism are observed. At autopsy, burns are found in the mucous membranes, and marked changes in the parenchymatous organs.

t: KMnO4 poisoning and the air limit
n: Now, KMnO4 poisoning and the air limit. The manganese content in the air of an enterprise must not exceed 0.0003 mg/l. When KMnO4 is used for criminal abortion, acute poisoning often occurs and leads to death. Poisoning also occurs when a concentrated KMnO4 solution is used for rinsing the mouth and in gynaecological practice. The LD50 for KMnO4 is 15-20 g.

Manganese content in organs. Manganese is one of the trace elements regularly found in the human body and necessary for life. 100 g of liver contains up to 0.4 mg of manganese, kidney up to 0.28 mg, and uterus up to 0.16 mg. Mn is detected by a qualitative reaction, so quantitative analysis is of decisive importance.

The confirmatory reaction of manganese is based on oxidation. Mn2+ is oxidised by potassium periodate and ammonium persulphate to pink-red permanganate. The reaction involves MnSO4 and (NH4)2S2O8 or KIO4, and the product is HMnO4. Both reactions are specific: other metals are oxidised but do not give such a product. The influence of the iron ion is eliminated by adding NaH2PO4, and that of the chloride ion by adding AgNO3.

We compare two ways of oxidising manganese. Mn2+ is oxidised by potassium periodate and ammonium persulphate to pink-red permanganate. Both reactions are specific; other metals do not give such a product. Measures against interfering ions: for iron, NaH2PO4; for chloride, AgNO3. Chromium, that is, Cr3+, gives an orange colour and interferes.

Separating manganese and chromium. The chromium ion interferes with the reaction: oxidised from Cr3+ to Cr6+, it gives an orange colour. A green colour of the mineralisate suggests, approximately, the presence of chromium. In such cases manganese is separated by extraction into the chloroform layer as diethyldithiocarbamate at pH = 8. Chromium remains in the aqueous layer.

t: Extracting Mn with DDTC and re-extraction
n: Extraction of Mn with DDTC and re-extraction are carried out in five steps. First, with DDTC at pH = 8, manganese passes into chloroform. Second, chromium remains in the aqueous layer. Third, with nitric acid Mn2+ is transferred back into the aqueous layer; this is re-extraction. Fourth, it is oxidised with periodate to Mn7+. Fifth, the resulting coloured solution is measured by PEC. The aqueous layer is tested for Mn2+.

Re-extraction and quantitative determination of manganese. Chromium remains in the aqueous solution, while manganese is separated from the chloroform layer by re-extraction with nitric acid. The aqueous layer is tested for Mn2+. The determination of the amount of Mn2+ is based on oxidation with potassium periodate to Mn7+. The resulting coloured solution is measured by PEC.

Uses of chromium compounds. They are widely used in leather tanning and in the textile industry, but are not used in medicine. They are also used in chromium plating of metals and in the production of matches, paints, and cine and photographic film. The reason chromium compounds are not used as drugs is that they act as very strong poisons.

t: Toxicity of chromium and signs of poisoning
n: Toxicity of chromium and signs of poisoning. Of the chromium compounds, the 6-valent ones are a stronger poison than the 3-valent ones. The LD50 of chromic anhydride is 0.2-1 g. When taken by mouth, the mucous membranes of the mouth, stomach and oesophagus are burned and stained yellow. The vomit contains blood. Cyanosis, collapse and weakening of cardiac activity are observed.

Post-mortem examination in chromium poisoning. At autopsy, the stomach and oesophagus are seen to be shrunken and reduced in size. In the stomach there is a blue-coloured mass; this is trivalent chromium. Destruction of the nasal septum is one of the main signs of chromium poisoning. The main part of chromium accumulates in the kidneys and liver.

Principles of chromium determination. If chromium is present in a biological specimen, the mineralisate is stained green. Although the chromium cation in the mineralisate is trivalent, it is converted to the 6-valent state when the cations are separated. The determination is based on the formation of perchromic acid and on the reaction with diphenylcarbazide. In both reactions, Cr3+ is oxidised to Cr6+. Iron is masked by adding NaH2PO4, and chloride by adding AgNO3.

Formation of perchromic acid. Although the chromium cation in the mineralisate is trivalent, it is converted to the 6-valent state when the cations are separated. Perchromic acid forms in the presence of H2Cr2O7 and H2O2. The reaction: H2Cr2O7 and 3 H2O2 give H2Cr2O10 and 3 H2O. The acid is blue and is easily extracted with ethyl acetate. Iron cations are masked by adding NaH2PO4, and the chloride anion by adding AgNO3.

t: Reactions of perchromic acid and diphenylcarbazide
n: Two reactions of Cr6+. In the formation of perchromic acid a blue colour appears, and it is easily extracted with ethyl acetate. With diphenylcarbazide, a red-violet colour forms. The amount of chromium is determined by measuring the compound formed with diphenylcarbazide by the PEC method.

The reaction of chromium with diphenylcarbazide. The determination of chromium is based on the formation of perchromic acid and on the reaction with diphenylcarbazide. Cr3+ is first oxidised to Cr6+. The oxidised mineralisate gives a red-violet compound with diphenylcarbazide. The amount of chromium is determined by measuring the resulting compound by the photoelectrocolorimetric method.

We compare the confirmatory reactions. Silver gives a yellow-golden colour with dithizone, AgCl is precipitated with NaCl, and microcrystals form in the ammonia complex. For copper, DDTC extraction and the reactions with tetrathiocyanatomercurate and yellow prussiate of potash are used; with pyridine thiocyanate an emerald-green colour appears. Manganese is oxidised with periodate and persulphate and gives a pink-red colour. Chromium is determined with perchromic acid and diphenylcarbazide, the colour being red-violet.

Interfering ions. In the determination of silver, mercury interferes with the dithizone reaction; it is distinguished with 0.5 N HCl. In the determination of copper with tetrathiocyanatomercurate, Fe, Co and Ni also form a coloured precipitate. In the determination of manganese, the chromium ion interferes: passing from Cr3+ to Cr6+ it gives an orange colour. Iron is masked with NaH2PO4, and chloride with AgNO3.

Measures for eliminating interfering ions. For silver, mercury dithizonate also gives a yellow-golden colour; we distinguish it with 0.5 N HCl. For copper, iron, cobalt and nickel also form a coloured precipitate with tetrathiocyanatomercurate. For manganese, iron is eliminated with NaH2PO4 and chloride with AgNO3, while chromium is separated with DDTC at pH = 8. In the determination of chromium too, iron is masked with NaH2PO4 and chloride with AgNO3.

Quantitative methods. Silver is determined by the volumetric method: titration with ammonium thiocyanate with an Fe(III) salt as indicator. Copper is determined as the DDTC complex by PEC or by titration with Trilon B; with murexide as indicator the colour changes from yellow to red. Manganese is oxidised with periodate to Mn7+ and measured by PEC. Chromium is determined with diphenylcarbazide by the PEC method.

Let us summarise. Silver is tested with dithizone, then AgCl is precipitated with NaCl and confirmed in the ammonia complex. Copper is isolated as the DDTC complex, while manganese is separated from chromium with DDTC at pH = 8. Chromium is oxidised to Cr6+ and determined with perchromic acid and diphenylcarbazide. For self-check, revise: the isolation schemes, interfering ions, quantitative methods and degrees of toxicity.
